samples.user_input: What are the limitations of both naive integer assignment and one-hot encoding when trying to represent a 50,000-word vocabulary and measure similarity between words?
reference_contexts: TRANSFORMER THEORY NOTES PAGE - 2 2. DISCRETE → CONTINUOUS The single most important shift in representing words ★The naive idea Give every word an integer: dog → 1 car → 2 house → 3 bus → 4 ★Will the machine learn from that ? With 4 words — yes. A network can memorise that 1 means dog. With 50,000 words — no. And that is the real scale. The integers imply an order and a magnitude that do not exist: nothing about language says bus is four times dog, or that house sits between car and bus. ⚠ The fatal flaw of discrete values You cannot compute cosine similarity between two integers. Similarity is deﬁned between vectors. With scalars there is no angle to measure, and therefore no notion of "these two words are alike". ★One-hot encoding — the ﬁrst ﬁx vocab = [dog, cat, car] dog = { 1 , 0, 0 } cat = { 0, 1 , 0 } car = { 0, 0, 1 } Now they are vectors — but every pair is orthogonal, so the cosine similarity between any two words is exactly 0. Dog and cat are as unrelated as dog and car. And with a 50,000-word vocabulary each vector is 50,000 long and 49,999 of those entries are zero. ★Continuous is the answer discrete : 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 continuous : 0.98, 0.72, 0.64, 0.78, … Dense ﬂoating-point numbers — float32, sometimes float16 — where a single word is 300 or 768 or 4096 numbers, all of them non- zero, each one a learned attribute. Every embedding you will ever use in 2026 is continuous. There is no such thing as a discrete embedding model. ONE-HOT — 1 useful number, 49,999 zeros … 49,992 more zeros DENSE — every number carries a learned attribute … 292 more, all non-zero COSINE SIMILARITY one-hot : always 0.00 — every word orthogonal dense : 0.87 for king/queen, 0.12 for king/pizza What lives inside those numbers Take king and queen. Some dimensions encode royalty, some family, some power, some history, some gender. Nobody labels them — the model discovers them. Because so many dimensions agree, the two vectors are close, and closeness is what we call context.
samples.reference: Based on the provided context, the limitations of both approaches are: **Naive Integer Assignment:** * **Fails at scale:** While a network can memorize 4 words, a machine cannot learn from integer assignments at the real scale of a 50,000-word vocabulary. * **Implies false order and magnitude:** Assigning integers implies relationships that do not exist in language (for example, falsely suggesting that "bus" (4) is four times "dog" (1), or that "house" (3) sits between "car" (2) and "bus" (4)). * **Cannot measure similarity:** You cannot compute cosine similarity between two integers because similarity is defined between vectors. With scalars, there is no angle to measure and therefore no way to capture the notion that two words are alike. **One-Hot Encoding:** * **Extremely sparse and long vectors:** With a 50,000-word vocabulary, each vector must be 50,000 entries long, consisting of only 1 useful number and 49,999 zeros. * **No meaningful similarity measurement:** Although the words are converted into vectors, every pair is orthogonal. As a result, the cosine similarity between any two words is always exactly 0 (0.00), making related words like "dog" and "cat" appear just as unrelated as "dog" and "car."

Because self-attention is permutation-equivariant — a dot product carries no information about where its operands sat. Without PE, "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" produce the same set of output vectors. Q · Why divide by √d_k? A dot product of d_k- dimensional vectors has variance d_k, so scores grow with dimension; large scores saturate softmax into a one-hot and kill the gradient. Dividing by √d_k restores unit variance so sharpness is independent of head size. Q · Why multi-head instead of one big head? One softmax can be sharp on one relationship. Splitting 512 into 8 × 64 gives eight independent views (syntax, coreference, position…) at the same total cost, and the output projection W_O recombines them.

samples.user_input: Compare the path lengths of self-attention, recurrent, and convolutional layers, and explain what self-attention gains from its path length despite being more expensive per layer when $n > d$.
reference_contexts: ★Complexity Layer type per layer path length Self-attention O(n²·d) O(1) Recurrent O(n·d²) O(n) Convolutional O(k·n·d²) O(log_k n) Attention is more expensive per layer when n > d — but its path length is 1, and that is what buys long-range dependency and full parallelism. ★Three more interview answers Q · Where do K, Q, V come from in cross- attention? K and V from the encoder's memory, Q from the decoder. No causal mask — the source is fully known. Q · Is attention symmetric? No. Once W_Q ≠ W_K, S_ij ≠ S_ji. A verb may attend strongly to its subject while the subject barely attends to the verb. Q · What is the bottleneck of the architecture? The n × n score matrix: O(n²) time and memory in sequence length. Every long-context method — sparse, linear, sliding-window, FlashAttention — attacks that one term. Q · Why layer norm and not batch norm? Layer norm normalises across features within one token, so it is independent of batch size and of the padding pattern. Batch norm's statistics would be corrupted by variable-length sequences. Q · What exactly does the mask do? It adds −∞ to the upper triangle of the score matrix before softmax, so e^(−∞)=0 and the future contributes nothing. It lets the model train on a whole sentence in parallel while behaving autoregressively. Where to go next These four sessions covered the theory.
